turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good morning. Mr. Ellison? I'm Dr. Shah. What brings you in?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Good morning, Doctor. Thank you for fitting me in. I have a cough that bothers me in the mornings, and I become short of breath more easily than I used to.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long has the cough been going on?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): That is hard to pin down. It has been since last winter, or perhaps the winter before. I cannot give you a proper date, I'm afraid.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Did the breathlessness start around then as well?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): More or less, yes. It came on gradually. I notice it on the stairs, and walking out to the car.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is the cough dry, or is there phlegm?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): In the morning there is some phlegm, clear, or a little gray. Later it is mostly a dry tickle. Bothersome, though I would not call it severe.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any blood in the phlegm?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No, Doctor. None that I have seen.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does it wake you at night?

[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): My wife insisted I tell you that I wake her coughing all night. Well, actually, I would not put it that way. It is chiefly in the morning. I do not believe I cough much once I am asleep.

[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): So, a morning cough with a little clear or gray phlegm, shortness of breath on the stairs and walking to the car, and you don't think the nighttime cough is really there. Is that right?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, that is a fair summary. Thank you.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain, fever at the moment, or swelling of the ankles?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain, and my ankles are not swollen. There is no fever now. I did have a fever during a chest infection some time ago, but that passed.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): I do, Doctor. About ten a day.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): And for how many years?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Since I was seventeen. I am sixty-four now. Um, well, actually, it is maybe twenty a day, not ten. I tend to minimize it, I'm sorry to say.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thank you for correcting that. Closer to a pack a day since your teens, then. Do you drink?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): A glass of wine with dinner, perhaps three evenings a week. Nothing more than that.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Still working?

[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): I retired last spring from the accounting firm. My wife and I live in the house on Maple. I still garden, though I must stop to catch my breath. The parking lot was terribly crowded this morning, though that is beside the point.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thoughtful of you. What inhalers are you on?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): I have the purple inhaler. I am embarrassed to admit I do not use it regularly.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): What is the purple inhaler called?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): It is Advair, the Diskus. I was told twice a day. In truth I take it when I remember, perhaps three mornings a week. I cannot recall the strength.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is there a rescue inhaler as well?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): The blue one. Albuterol, ProAir, I believe. Two puffs, I think, when I get winded. Lately that is three or four times a day if I walk any distance.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): You're not certain it is two puffs?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Not entirely, no. It might be two. I have never been very precise about it.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Other medicines, day to day?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): A small white pill for my blood pressure. Lisinopril, ten milligrams, by mouth, every morning. I have taken it for years.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): You mentioned a chest infection. When was that?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): I cannot date it properly. Around the holidays, or after the new year. I truly do not know which.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): How did it present?

[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): There was fever, the cough got heavier, and the phlegm turned yellow. Urgent care gave me a Z-pack. The fever and the yellow phlegm settled afterward. The morning cough never really went away.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any wheezing?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): I wheezed during that illness. Now only if I hurry. A little whistling in the chest.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Past surgeries? Anyone in the family with lung disease?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): I have never had an operation. My father had emphysema. He was a heavy smoker too. He passed away some years ago.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Medication allergies?

[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): I do not believe so. Though, um, there may have been a rash with penicillin when I was a boy. I cannot remember it myself, so I am unsure it is even true. The Z-pack caused me no difficulty.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Then I'll note a possible penicillin allergy as uncertain, not confirmed. Let me listen to your chest.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Of course. Please go ahead.

[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Scattered wheezes on both sides, a bit more on the right. No crackles. No ankle swelling. Your blood pressure is 138 over 82, pulse 78, respirations 18, and your oxygen is 94 percent on room air, which is a little lower than I like.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): I see. That oxygen figure is disappointing, though not entirely a surprise.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): The spirometry from this morning shows an FEV1 of 1.62 liters, 58 percent of predicted, FVC 3.05 liters, 76 percent predicted, and the ratio is 0.53. That is obstruction.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Are those numbers as poor as they sound, Doctor?

[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): They fit a working impression of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, given the smoking and the morning cough. I am not calling that final. I also would not rule out that part of the breathlessness is still the tail of the chest infection.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): I had hoped it was merely the infection lingering. I do understand.

[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): Use the Advair every morning and every evening, not just when you remember. I am going to prescribe a nicotine patch, 21 milligrams once a day, to help you cut down, and I will refer you to the state quitline.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): I am willing to try the patch. I have meant to stop for a long while. The garden will have to wait on my lungs, I suppose. A silly thought.

[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): We might do a chest CT if the cough and the breathlessness do not settle over the next couple of months, though not today. I do want a chest x-ray while you are here, with the smoking history and the cough that stayed on. Let's see you back in six weeks to go over the film, the patch, and the daily inhaler. If you cough up blood or the breathing gets sharply worse, come sooner or go to the emergency room.

vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.
hedged_plan: the doctor hedges ('we might do a scan if it does not settle', 'let's see in two weeks'). Conditional vs planned status must follow the words.
